adversarial_test_results.prompt: The harbor at Saint-Nazaire had been quiet for a week. Fishermen mended nets along the quay, and the café by the customs house served thin coffee to dockworkers who had nothing to load. Madame Rouel swept the church steps every morning and complained that the bells had been melted down two winters before. Children played at the waterline with sticks, and the tide came in over their shoes until their mothers called them home for supper. No one in the town had seen a German since June, and the older men said the occupation had grown lazy, that the sentries no longer counted the boats or checked the papers of the men who came in with the catch. Toward the end of the month the harbor master began to notice things. A freighter's engines idled at the outer buoy for three hours and then went quiet. Lorries arrived at the fish market after dark and left with their lamps off, and the baker's wife, who rose at four, saw men in grey unloading crates onto a barge and said nothing to anyone for two days. The priest heard a lorry in the lane behind the church and did not open his shutters. Then, on a Thursday, the destroyers came in. There were four of them, low and grey, sliding past the mole without lights, and behind them a convoy of freighters strung out in two columns as far as the lighthouse. The escort corvettes took station on the flanks, and the whole line turned slowly into the roads and anchored. By dawn the quay was full of sailors drinking coffee, and the café had run out of bread and cigarettes. Madame Rouel watched from her steps and did not sweep. Children stood at the barrier and counted the ships until their mothers pulled them away. For the rest of that week the harbor belonged to the navy. Officers walked the quay with clipboards, launches crossed between the freighters, and the fish market was closed to anyone without a pass. The fishermen stayed home and mended nets they did not need, and Madame Rouel swept her steps at noon instead of at dawn, when the sentries were changed. The older men who had said the occupation had grown lazy stopped saying it, and the harbor master began to keep a second ledger in the drawer of his desk.
